title: HS2: Can Britain Finally Get Its Railway Back on Track?
label: 14 September 2026 · HS2 costs, delays and Euston
summary: MPs questioned senior transport officials about the soaring cost of HS2, the high-speed railway between London and Birmingham, and the long-delayed redevelopment of Euston station. The railway is now expected to cost between £87.7 billion and £102.7 billion, with full services unlikely before 2040. HS2's new chief executive said the project had suffered from incomplete designs, poorly structured contracts and inadequate management, but argued that a major overhaul was producing results. Officials defended the railway's potential to relieve overcrowding and improve connections, while acknowledging uncertainty over future passenger demand, costs and contracts. MPs challenged whether the benefits justified the expense, questioned the estimates for cancelling the project and raised concerns about communities and landowners affected by years of disruption. Euston's plans and funding also remain unsettled. The central message was that management has improved, but delivering the railway within the latest estimates is far from guaranteed.

speakers.label: Chair
speakers.name: Sarah Olney

speakers.label: Ruth Cadbury

glossary.definition: High Speed Two, the high-speed railway being built between London and Birmingham, with trains intended to continue onto existing lines.
High Speed One, the railway connecting London with the Channel Tunnel and international rail services.
The major London railway construction project that created the Elizabeth line.
The independent public body that investigates how well central government uses public money.
Government guidance on how to assess the costs, benefits and risks of public projects.
The planned public body intended to bring together responsibility for planning and managing Britain's railways.
The organisation created to coordinate the redevelopment of Euston's railway stations, transport connections and surrounding area.
An exceptionally large government project that receives special oversight and greater flexibility in how it is managed.
Government rules requiring certain surplus properties to be offered back to former owners before being sold to someone else.

chapters.title: 1. Why should anyone trust the latest costs?
chapters.takeaway: HS2's leadership says it has rebuilt the project plan after discovering serious failures, but the latest cost and completion estimates still contain considerable uncertainty.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: HS2 has become an example of how not to run a major project. The latest estimate is £87.7 billion to £102.7 billion, with £46.8 billion already spent. Full services may not begin until 2040 to 2043. We've heard revised forecasts before. Why should we believe these figures won't rise again?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: We recognise how badly this programme has gone. The National Audit Office, which examines government spending, has acknowledged progress in identifying what went wrong and improving the management. But it's also warned us not to rush into approving a final plan before we're confident it can be delivered.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: When I arrived in December 2024, the programme wasn't properly coordinated. We didn't have a reliable picture of what had been built or what remained, and we couldn't rely on the cost figures. The Department, HS2 and the contractors weren't working to a shared plan. We needed a fundamental overhaul.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: We found three main causes. Construction started before the designs were sufficiently developed, so the amount of work and the risks were badly underestimated. The contracts left HS2 carrying most of the financial risk. And HS2 itself didn't manage the programme well enough. Those were failures of the overall system, despite the hard work of the people involved.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: We've now examined the remaining work in detail, identified what was missing and put the activities into a workable order. We're applying lessons from Crossrail, although HS2 is much larger and more complicated. Our aim is to open the first stretch, from Old Oak Common in west London to Birmingham, between 2036 and 2039. We're deliberately showing a broad range of possible costs and dates rather than pretending we know exactly what will happen.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But you're still negotiating with contractors. How can you finalise the plan while important agreements remain outstanding?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: There are seven major existing contracts: four for the main construction work, two for stations and one for trains. We've reached revised agreements on two construction contracts, with EKFB and Align. We're working closely with the other two construction contractors, BBV and SCS, and hope to reach agreements before Christmas. We expect progress on the stations and trains by March 2027, but I can't guarantee those outcomes.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: We're also preparing a single, detailed plan covering costs, dates and the order of construction. We'd like that ready by Christmas, and I'm confident we can have it by April 2027. But if independent checks find problems, we'll take longer. The Department, HS2 and contractors must all understand what they're expected to deliver. A further stage will deal with the remaining contract disagreements.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: We need a backup plan if some contractors don't agree. Mark is making progress, but we can't build the future of the railway around the assumption that every negotiation succeeds. We need to be capable of managing the programme whichever way those negotiations end.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: The cost estimates are intended to cover the problems we can reasonably anticipate, including the possibility of failing to reach new contracts. They don't cover extraordinary events such as wars, a pandemic or extreme inflation. There will be uncertainty right up to completion. Our responsibility is to manage it, while trying to deliver towards the lower end of the estimated cost range.

chapters.title: 2. Slower trains could mean an earlier opening
chapters.takeaway: Officials argue that dropping unusually high speeds and automated driving will make HS2 easier to test and open, with relatively little loss of benefit for passengers.

turns.speaker: Ruth Cadbury
turns.text: You've decided to reduce the planned train speed to around 300 kilometres an hour. How confident are you that this will save money and reduce risk? What will passengers lose?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: The Transport Secretary wanted to remove unnecessary technical difficulties without losing the main benefits. For London to Birmingham, the lower speed adds roughly three minutes compared with the original plan. Passengers would still save about 30 minutes compared with today's conventional trains.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: The original design aimed for 360 kilometres an hour. That involves technology and testing that haven't been proven in regular European high-speed services. At 300 to 320 kilometres an hour, we can use established technology similar to that in France, Spain, Japan and Italy. That's a much more dependable route to opening the railway.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: We've also removed the requirement for computers to control the trains automatically. Drivers will operate them, as they do on other high-speed railways. Automated driving exists on some other lines, but not in the form we would need here. Developing and testing it would add major difficulties. The railway can still run its planned 10 trains an hour, and its design won't prevent an increase to 16 in the future.

turns.speaker: Ruth Cadbury
turns.text: Does that mean we're sacrificing something passengers might otherwise have benefited from later?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: Potentially, but keeping the original requirements might have meant another one or two years and £2 billion to £3 billion of testing. I don't believe we could have opened around 2037 with those requirements. Future generations can introduce more advanced technology if it becomes practical. It doesn't make sense to hold up the railway now for something that might have changed completely in 20 or 30 years.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: Our assessment is that the overall economic benefits change very little. There's a small loss from longer journeys, but that can be offset by opening earlier. Manually driven trains may need more staff, while lower speeds could reduce electricity use. The important lesson is to deal with foreseeable technical problems now rather than discover them when we're trying to open the railway.

chapters.title: 3. What will taxpayers actually get?
chapters.takeaway: Officials say HS2's biggest benefits are more reliable services and extra railway capacity, but MPs question whether future passenger demand justifies the enormous cost.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: We're spending an extraordinary amount of money on a railway between London and Birmingham. It was originally presented as a way to improve opportunities in the north, but that wider scheme has been cut back. Meanwhile, technology and home working may reduce the need to travel. What benefits will taxpayers actually get?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: It's not mainly about faster journeys. The West Coast Main Line, the existing railway serving Birmingham and the north-west, is extremely crowded. Last year, only 57% of Avanti trains arrived within three minutes of schedule, against an industry average of 85%. The rail regulator also rejected three applications for new services because there wasn't room for them. HS2 would move long-distance trains onto a separate route and free up space for other passengers and freight.

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: At the busiest times, the number of long-distance seats available each hour from London to Birmingham would rise from fewer than 800 to more than 4,000. Passengers on the existing railway should also benefit because it would have more room to operate reliably.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: We're expecting journey times between London and Birmingham to fall by about 30 minutes and an increase in capacity for other services in the south. But we need to decide how to use the space HS2 releases. There's also the possibility of new development around stations. Across Old Oak Common, Interchange and Birmingham Curzon Street, our estimates suggest around 49,000 additional jobs and 60,000 homes could be created.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: But how do you know people will use it? Working patterns have changed considerably since the railway was first proposed. Without sufficient passengers, those supposed benefits won't materialise.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: Rail travel has broadly recovered since the pandemic, although leisure travel now makes up a larger share. We're forecasting annual passenger growth of roughly 1% to 2% over the next 25 years, which is more cautious than previous expectations. Our current assessment puts the benefits at about £36 billion. Demand could be higher, but it is genuinely uncertain. Next year's updated assessment will show what happens under different growth scenarios.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: I still struggle to see the logic. We're getting a reduced railway at enormous expense. You mention freight, but Britain relies heavily on road transport, and making more use of rail freight would require further investment. I'm not convinced by the case you're presenting.

turns.speaker: Ruth Cadbury
turns.text: Freight companies are already desperate for more space on the existing railway. Do we know how many extra freight trains could run once HS2 opens, including if the high-speed network eventually extends towards Manchester?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: We don't have a figure yet. Freight trains won't run on HS2 itself. The question is how to use the space freed on the existing network. That will need to be worked through by Great British Railways, including consultation on the balance between freight and passenger services.

chapters.title: 4. Bad contracts and the cost of cancelling
chapters.takeaway: The original contracts left taxpayers exposed to escalating costs, while a disputed estimate of the cost of cancellation became a major point of disagreement.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: As someone who's worked as a contractor, it looks to me as though the Government started without knowing exactly what it wanted to build. The contracts then allowed construction firms to recover their costs rather than genuinely commit to a fixed price. Is that a fair assessment?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: Yes, broadly. When work began, the designs weren't mature enough for contractors to accept the financial risk. They weren't going to put their companies at risk on something so uncertain. HS2 therefore took much of that risk itself. It should have recognised the potential costs much more clearly. That's an important lesson for future projects.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: But once you've signed contracts like that, you're in a weak position. Did political pressure to get construction started cause this? And how much can you really change the arrangements now?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: I can't tell you what motivated the original decisions because I wasn't there. But the contracts certainly gave contractors too little reason to minimise spending. We can't completely undo that. What we can do is change the incentives so that finishing the work quickly and controlling costs benefit both sides.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: With EKFB and Align, we've settled earlier disputes, fixed the fees they receive rather than letting those grow automatically with spending, and introduced rewards for finishing sooner. We want the main construction work finished in 2029 so track installation can begin in March 2030. We're trying to reach similar agreements with BBV and SCS.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: The National Audit Office discusses potential savings of £2 billion. Are those real savings, or could the contractors still end up costing us more?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: It's mainly about avoiding future costs and risks, not £2 billion already saved. There's still uncertainty. But we're seeing encouraging results. For example, EKFB was supposed to move 16 million cubic metres of earth this financial year and had already moved 15 million by last week. Better designs and favourable weather have helped too, so I wouldn't claim it's all because of the new contract.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: One of our greatest risks is simply that construction takes too long. Every additional period on site costs money and delays the installation of railway equipment. We want contractors to care about public spending and have a clear reason to finish sooner. Performance from the firms that have signed revised agreements is encouraging.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: I also question the calculation of what it would cost to cancel HS2. The estimate is now £33 billion to £58 billion, whereas an estimate in 2023 was around £11 billion. The Department and HS2 appear to have assessed cancellation themselves. Why wasn't that independently verified?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: We asked for an assessment proportionate to the decision being made. There isn't a detailed plan for dismantling the railway, and creating one would have taken considerable effort away from completing it. We had to balance the value of more detailed calculations against the work needed to deliver the project.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: We estimated the cost of restoring the land and dealing with what had already been built by using a range equivalent to 35% to 55% of expenditure, then added 66% to allow for costs we couldn't yet identify. We also face possible contractor claims, and restoring the land could be extremely difficult. In my judgment, the estimate may actually be conservative.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: But 66% is the maximum allowance suggested in the Government's Green Book guidance. That's a subjective choice, and it makes cancellation look more expensive. I'm concerned that the figures could have been chosen to support the decision to continue.

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: It is a judgment. But HS2 has repeatedly underestimated costs, and we have no comparable example of dismantling a project of this scale. Given the uncertainty, we considered that allowance appropriate.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Why announce that you're continuing before finishing the contract negotiations? Surely keeping cancellation as a genuine possibility would give you more bargaining power.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: We considered that. But with tens of thousands of people working on HS2 and around £25 million being spent every day, I don't think contractors would have believed cancellation was a credible threat. They might even have made more money from ending their contracts under the old arrangements. I'd also be cautious about the £11 billion figure from 2023, given how much HS2 underestimated costs then. Around £25 billion more has since been spent on the infrastructure.

chapters.title: 5. The unfinished railway beyond Birmingham
chapters.takeaway: Cutting back the original network has created problems for train capacity and connections, and officials are still working out how HS2 will fit into the wider railway.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: HS1 connects London with international rail services, and St Pancras is very close to Euston. Have you considered linking the two high-speed railways? It could create more opportunities for travel across Europe and increase the value of HS2.

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: That possibility has been examined before. But successive Governments have reduced HS2's scope, and the immediate priority is addressing overcrowding on the West Coast Main Line. The Government wants to complete the railway to Euston and improve the stations and surrounding area. That's where the focus is now.

turns.speaker: Ruth Cadbury
turns.text: Cancelling the railway north of Birmingham created another problem. The longer trains originally ordered for HS2 can't run on parts of the existing railway further north. If you simply use shorter trains, you could lose the extra seats the project is supposed to provide. How are you resolving that?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: You're right that shorter trains would reduce capacity if we did nothing else. We're working with the manufacturer to find a solution that operates on the new railway and the existing network beyond Birmingham, without blocking future expansion. We're also discussing it with the organisations that manage and operate the railway. We hope to reach a decision during the next year, but I can't give an exact date.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: The discussions with the train manufacturer are going well, but the problem hasn't been resolved yet. We need to finish those negotiations rather than speculate about the outcome.

chapters.title: 6. Who's making sure mistakes aren't repeated?
chapters.takeaway: New oversight arrangements and experienced staff have improved management, but MPs warn that more committees and procedures won't automatically deliver a successful railway.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: HS2 now has special oversight because it's classified as a mega-project. Has that actually changed the way decisions are made?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: Yes. The previous system had too many overlapping stages of approval, and it wasn't always clear who was responsible for making decisions. We now have more direct scrutiny, including independent experts, a board examining the Department's oversight of HS2 and a group of Ministers making major decisions. We believe that's helped the work to develop a more realistic plan.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: Isn't there a risk that you've simply replaced one complicated, ineffective system with another?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: That's a fair challenge. The idea is to make decisions at the right level. Ministers consider big choices, such as train speed. Mark and I formally review progress every month, while our senior teams meet weekly to deal with problems. If something can't be resolved, we can take it to the appropriate board or Ministers. The test is whether those arrangements actually help construction progress.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: And does HS2 have enough experienced people to make the new plans work? What happens if the organisational problems return?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: We've strengthened the senior management team, including bringing in dedicated leaders for contracts and project delivery. We've also moved 300 roles away from central administration and towards the people managing construction. We're attracting experienced staff and don't currently face major recruitment difficulties.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: But hiring good people isn't enough. We need regular measurements that show whether the organisation itself is functioning properly, not just how much concrete has been poured or track laid. Previously, weaknesses developed without being detected early enough. We won't consider the overhaul complete until we're satisfied that HS2 has the people and systems needed to maintain the new plan.

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: We're also committed to reporting openly to Parliament every six months. The next report is due before the end of 2026. Better relationships between the Department and HS2 matter, but Parliament must be able to see what is actually happening.

chapters.title: 7. Euston: A station without a final price
chapters.takeaway: Euston's redevelopment could cost around £8 billion, but its design and funding remain uncertain, and officials insist that all the connected stations must be planned together.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: Turning to Euston, the railway station and surrounding redevelopment were estimated at £3.8 billion in March 2026, but the potential cost is now around £8 billion. Is that a reliable figure?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: Not yet. Euston's cost estimates are much less developed than the main HS2 estimates. We've tried to deliver this project twice before and failed. We now have an agreed outline of how the site should be arranged and a new Euston Delivery Company to bring the organisations together. But we need a detailed design before we can produce a dependable cost and timetable.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: The crucial lesson is that we can't treat the new HS2 station, the existing mainline station, the Underground and the surrounding development as separate projects. They're all packed into one area and depend on each other. The Euston Delivery Company brings together HS2, Network Rail, which manages existing railway infrastructure, and Transport for London, which runs London's transport services. Ministers and local government also have a role in agreeing the overall plan.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: How established is this new company? How many people does it employ, and when will it have its leadership in place?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: There are about 30 posts at present. It's currently part of the Department for Transport, but we expect it to become a separate public organisation during the autumn. We're appointing its chief executive and arranging to bring in specialists from the partner organisations. The chief executive will then need to decide what additional expertise is required.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: Will the new leadership have a deadline for producing a full plan? Without one, couldn't the project simply drift again?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: We want them to challenge the current timetable, which has trains running from Euston between 2040 and 2043. That's an incredibly long time, particularly for the local community. But I won't impose an arbitrary deadline that encourages another unrealistic plan. There are likely to be four or five years of planning before construction of the station itself begins. Getting the design, costs and responsibilities right now is essential.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: And where will the money come from? You're talking about public funding, but also private investment in the station and surrounding property.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: Funding should follow a credible plan, rather than being agreed before we know what we're building. We expect some direct taxpayer funding, and we're exploring private investment in the HS2 station, money from developing land around Euston and ways of using additional tax revenues generated by that development. We hope to make progress alongside the next government spending review, but there's still a lot to work through.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: Are you learning from other major projects about how to make these private funding arrangements work without exposing taxpayers to more risks?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: Yes. We're working with outside experts and the Treasury. Around 70 organisations responded to our early discussions with potential investors. They're particularly concerned about inflation and about delays caused by other parts of the Euston project. We need to establish who carries those risks before inviting formal bids. We won't enter into a private funding deal unless it offers acceptable value for taxpayers.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: Euston's redevelopment appears separately from HS2 in the Government's list of major projects. Shouldn't it have its own mega-project status and oversight?

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: At present it benefits from HS2's mega-project arrangements, and we don't believe that prevents us from managing it properly. Whether it should eventually be classified separately is something we'll discuss with the Treasury and the Government's infrastructure specialists.

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: What's important is that separate classifications don't lead to the projects working against each other. Euston is essential to the successful completion of HS2. We must keep them coordinated, even if the formal arrangements change later.

turns.speaker: Ruth Cadbury
turns.text: I want to make sure passengers aren't forgotten. Most people arriving at Euston will continue by Underground, bus, taxi, bicycle or another train. Some will need to reach St Pancras. Walking distances and accessibility matter, especially for people with luggage or limited mobility. Who's making sure all those connections work?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: That's precisely why the transport organisations need to agree how the station will operate before finalising its design. We're looking at bus and taxi connections, movement between stations and even practical issues such as whether passengers have to pass through multiple ticket barriers. There will be difficult choices between what we'd ideally provide and what we can afford. The partners will need to agree that their requirements have been addressed.

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: Transport for London understands how important Euston is to journeys across London, including connections towards St Pancras. We're also working with the operators of the existing station to make improvements for passengers now, rather than expecting everyone to wait until the full redevelopment is finished.

chapters.title: 8. The communities and landowners left waiting
chapters.takeaway: MPs pressed officials to reduce disruption around Euston and return land no longer needed for HS2, while a request for an independent review of cancellation costs remained unresolved.

turns.speaker: Ruth Cadbury
turns.text: People living and running businesses around Euston have already endured years of construction and uncertainty. What are you doing to reduce the impact, particularly when the redevelopment is going to take so much longer?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: We've provided around £2 million through HS2 to help affected communities, and Camden Council has contributed roughly £3.5 million, particularly for measures to deal with noise. The Euston Delivery Company will coordinate how the organisations work with residents. We're conscious that these problems have lasted a long time and that support may need to continue.

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: Drummond Street has suffered particularly badly. One useful improvement is taking excavated material away by rail: one train a day removes the need for around 50 lorry journeys. We're also supporting local skills and construction employment. But the community has been badly disrupted, and that's not going to disappear quickly. We need to keep working directly with residents and businesses.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: HS2 also bought enormous amounts of land and property, much of it for railway routes that have since been cancelled. People's lives were turned upside down. Why has it taken so long to start returning property, particularly where the Crichel Down rules say former owners should be offered the chance to buy it back?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: On the cancelled eastern route towards Leeds, we have about 500 properties that are no longer needed. Around 300 fall under those rules. The other 200 were acquired through different arrangements, sometimes because owners voluntarily sold them to us. An appointed agent is preparing a disposal plan, which we expect in October. We'd like some properties on the market this year, with more activity in the new year.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: But delaying sales creates other risks. Property values could fall, and holding empty homes or unused farmland costs money. Why not get on with returning what's no longer needed?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: We do need to move, but selling hundreds of properties at once could depress local prices and harm both residents and taxpayers. We also have to decide what land might still be needed for future rail construction. While we retain property, we maintain it and try to rent it out at market rates. About 60% of the relevant properties are rented. Some agricultural land is still being used by its former owners under lease.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Are taxpayers losing money through all this property management and the fees paid to outside agents?

turns.speaker: Dean Creamer
turns.text: Rental income broadly covers the running costs of maintaining properties, although the wider arrangements still cost money because some buildings need investment. Ministers monitor this closely, and we're trying to avoid unnecessary spending while disposing of property as responsibly and quickly as possible.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: What about land you only needed temporarily? When will that go back?

turns.speaker: Mark Wild
turns.text: That work has started on the former route north of Birmingham. We have around 450 investigation boreholes to fill and land to restore. We expect to complete that within 18 months. Land bought permanently needs further decisions, but returning the temporary land is already under way.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Finally, will you agree to an independent review of the estimated cost of cancelling HS2? I think taxpayers deserve confirmation that the figures aren't simply coming from the organisations responsible for delivering it.

turns.speaker: Jo Shanmugalingam
turns.text: If the Committee recommends that, we'll consider it with Ministers. But the Government has decided to continue with the railway, and our priority is to deliver it safely, as quickly as reasonably possible and at the lowest reasonable cost. We've already made a judgment about how much work to devote to estimating cancellation costs. We'll consider the Committee's recommendations, but I'm not committing to a new review today.
